name: Crater Lake
title: Crater Lake Volcano: Mount Mazama, Eruption & Lake Depth
description: Crater Lake in Oregon: the eruption that collapsed Mount Mazama 7,700 years ago, the deepest lake in the US, Wizard Island and the alert level now.
since_check: **Not erupting. Volcano Alert Level Normal, Aviation Color Code Green.** The weekly update of the USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory of November 20, 2026, read on {read_date}, put every Cascade volcano, Crater Lake among them, at normal background activity.[[cvo]] The Smithsonian’s list has no eruption after about {last_year}.[[gvp]]
lede: Crater Lake, in the Cascade Range of Oregon, fills the caldera of Mount Mazama, a volcano about 12,000 ft (3,660 m) high whose top collapsed in a series of explosive eruptions about 7,700 years ago. Its lake is the deepest in the United States, and its later eruptions built Wizard Island and a lava dome under the water. Below: its state now, the eruption that made the caldera, the lake and its island, whether it could erupt again and every eruption on record.
answer: **Crater Lake is not erupting.** The USGS keeps it at Volcano Alert Level Normal, and the last eruption on the Smithsonian’s list came about {last_year}.[[cvo]][[gvp]] The lake fills the caldera of Mount Mazama, which collapsed in a series of explosive eruptions about 7,700 years ago, and at **{depth_ft} ft ({depth_m} m)** it is the deepest lake in the United States.[[usgs]][[npsplace]]

paras: Crater Lake lies in the southern Cascade Range of Oregon, in Klamath County, inside Crater Lake National Park.[[gvp]][[usgs]][[npsplace]] The Smithsonian places the volcano at {coords}.[[gvp]]
The lake averages more than 5 miles (8 km) across. It fills a caldera 5 by 6 miles (8 by 10 km) wide, the collapsed top of the volcano called Mount Mazama.[[npsplace]][[usgs]]

sections.h: Is Crater Lake still an active volcano?
paras: It is not erupting. The USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory put Crater Lake at Volcano Alert Level Normal and Aviation Color Code Green in its weekly update of November 20, 2026.[[cvo]]
It still counts as active: the USGS rates its threat potential very high on the scale of its National Volcano Early Warning System.[[usgs]]

About 7,700 years ago, a series of explosive eruptions made Mount Mazama, then about 12,000 ft (3,660 m) high, collapse into a basin more than 0.6 miles (1 km) deep.[[usgs]][[npsnature]] It was the largest explosive eruption in the Cascades in the past 400,000 years, the USGS says.[[ofr]]

The Smithsonian counts it among the largest eruptions known on Earth since the last ice age: its ash reached as far as Canada, and its pyroclastic flows traveled 25 miles (40 km) from the volcano.[[gvp]] It rates the eruption VEI {max_vei} and dates it by an ice core to about {largest_year}.[[gvp]]

**{depth_ft} ft ({depth_m} m)** at its deepest, which makes it the deepest lake in the United States, the Park Service says.[[npsplace]] Its walls rise up to {wall_ft} ft ({wall_m} m) above the water, and its surface lies about {lake_ft} ft ({lake_m} m) above sea level.[[npsplace]][[npsguide]]

Rain and melted snow fill it, about 42 ft (13 m) of snow in an average year, and evaporation and seepage keep it from rising higher; its level changes only a few feet from year to year.[[npsnature]][[npsplace]][[npsguide]]

A cinder cone that grew on the caldera floor within a few hundred years of the collapse.[[gvp]] It rises {island_ft} ft ({island_m} m) above the lake and has a crater about 300 ft (90 m) across and 90 ft (27 m) deep at its top.[[npsplace]]
Its neighbor of the same age, Merriam Cone, never reached the surface. The last eruption on the list, about {last_year}, built a small lava dome beneath the lake east of Wizard Island.[[gvp]]

sections.note: This page is a record, not a safety guide. For alerts, follow the USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory.
paras: The USGS expects so: the volcanic center will be active in the future, it says, though it has had no significant eruption in about the past 5,000 years.[[usgshaz]] Future eruptions will likely come inside the caldera and probably beneath the water’s surface.[[usgshaz]]
The hazards it lists include steam-driven explosions, falling ash, pyroclastic flows, lahars and rockfalls.[[usgshaz]] NOAA’s database of significant eruptions has no entry for Crater Lake.[[noaa]]

sections.h: How often has Crater Lake erupted?
paras: Rarely, and not for a long time. The Smithsonian’s list has {n_all} eruptions, the oldest about {oldest} and the last about {last_year}, {quiet_span} ago.[[gvp]] Mount Mazama itself was built between about 420,000 and 40,000 years ago from at least five overlapping volcanoes.[[gvp]]

sections.h: How high is Crater Lake’s rim?
paras: The volcano’s highest point is **{summit_ft} ft ({summit_m} m)** above sea level, by the Smithsonian and the USGS.[[gvp]][[usgs]] The Park Service names Hillman Peak, 8,151 ft (2,484 m), as the highest point on the rim and Mount Scott, 8,929 ft (2,722 m), as the highest in the park.[[npsnature]]
The land around the volcano lies at about {ground_ft} ft ({ground_m} m), so its top stands about {rise_ft} ft ({rise_m} m) above its surroundings.[[etopo]]

sections.h: What type of volcano is Crater Lake?
paras: A caldera, the Smithsonian and the USGS say: the collapsed remains of Mount Mazama, a cluster of overlapping shield volcanoes and stratovolcanoes of andesite and dacite.[[gvp]][[usgs]] Its main rock on the Smithsonian’s list is {rock}.[[gvp]]

The Smithsonian’s record for Crater Lake has **{n_all} confirmed eruptions**, all before written history: {n_rc_word} dated by radiocarbon, {n_tephra_word} by layers of ash and one by an ice core.[[gvp]]

faq: Is Crater Lake an active volcano?
The USGS expects the volcanic center to erupt again, most likely inside the caldera. It is not erupting now: the USGS had it at Volcano Alert Level Normal in its update of November 20, 2026.
When did Crater Lake last erupt?
About {last_year}, by the Smithsonian’s list, when a small lava dome grew beneath the lake east of Wizard Island.
{depth_ft} ft ({depth_m} m) at its deepest, by the Park Service, which makes it the deepest lake in the United States.
Mount Mazama, a volcano about 12,000 ft high, collapsed during a series of explosive eruptions about 7,700 years ago, and rain and snow filled the caldera it left.
A cinder cone that grew on the caldera floor after the collapse; it rises {island_ft} ft ({island_m} m) above the lake.
About 12,000 ft (3,660 m) before the collapse, by the Park Service.

calc: **{quiet_span} ago:** counted from about {last_year}, the last eruption on the Smithsonian’s list, to today, rounded to the nearest 100 years. The Smithsonian’s own summary puts that eruption about 4,200 years ago, the Park Service about 4,800 and the USGS volcano page 6,600; this page uses the date on the list.
**About {rise_ft} ft ({rise_m} m) above its surroundings:** the summit height minus the median height of the land 14 to 16 km from the summit in NOAA’s ETOPO 2022 grid, rounded to 50 m.

**{depth_ft} ft ({depth_m} m) deep:** the Park Service’s figure; the USGS gives 594 m (1,949 ft) and the Smithsonian 600 m. The lake’s surface, {lake_ft} ft in the Park Service’s guide, is converted to meters.
Miles and feet are converted from the metric figures in the sources and rounded, except where the source prints feet.
